# Feedback control (governor, negative feedback) (`feedback_control`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: helped by differential_equations, piston_pump, windmill, vacuum_tube
- Core idea: A machine can regulate itself if it measures its own result, compares it with the wanted value and uses the difference to act against the error. A float in a cistern closes the inlet valve as the water rises. Two weights spinning with an engine fly outwards when it runs too fast and close the steam valve (centrifugal governor). A rod that expands with heat closes the damper of a furnace (thermostat). The danger is overcorrection: if the action is too strong or comes too late, the system swings to and fro ever more violently (hunting), so strength and delay of the correction must be matched. In amplifiers, feeding a fraction of the output back in opposition to the input gives up some amplification and makes the rest steady and less distorted within the amplifier’s operating range.
- Pitfalls:
  - Too strong or too delayed a correction, which produces oscillation instead of steadiness
  - Connecting it the wrong way round: positive feedback drives the machine to its limit or makes an amplifier howl
  - Expecting a simple governor to hold speed exactly; with proportional action alone a small error always remains under load
  - Crediting Watt with the centrifugal governor; he took it in 1788 from windmills, where millwrights already used it
- History: greece: c. 270 BC – Ktesibios of Alexandria's float valve keeps the inflow of a water clock constant; 1st c. AD Hero's float regulators; islamic: 9th c. – the Banu Musa's Book of Ingenious Devices uses float valves and level controls; 1206 al-Jazari; europe: c. 1620 – Drebbel's thermostat for a furnace and incubator; 1745 Edmund Lee's windmill fantail; 1787 Mead's centrifugal regulator for mills; 1788 Watt's engine governor; 1868 Maxwell, On Governors; 1877 Routh's stability criterion; americas: 1922 – Minorsky's three-term (PID) ship steering; 1927 Harold Black's negative-feedback amplifier at Bell Labs, published 1934; 1932 Nyquist's stability criterion; 1940–1945 Bode's design methods; 1948 Wiener's Cybernetics
- Read:
  - Otto Mayr, The Origins of Feedback Control (1970)
  - James Clerk Maxwell, On Governors, Proceedings of the Royal Society 16 (1868)
  - David A. Mindell, Between Human and Machine: Feedback, Control, and Computing before Cybernetics (2002)
